lesson.title: Where the Keys Live: Understanding Crypto Wallets
lesson.summary: A wallet does not hold coins at all; it holds the private keys that prove ownership of coins recorded on the blockchain, and the software that uses those keys to sign transactions.
lesson.body:
A wallet does not hold cryptocurrency the way a physical wallet holds cash. Every unit of a cryptocurrency that exists is recorded as an entry on the blockchain itself, in the transaction history maintained by the network's shared ledger. What a wallet actually stores is a private key, or more commonly today a seed phrase that can regenerate many private keys, along with the software needed to use that key to prove ownership and authorize spending. Losing the wallet does not destroy the coins; it destroys your ability to prove they are yours.

To see why this matters, recall how public key cryptography works. A private key is a large random number kept secret by its owner, and a public key is mathematically derived from it in a way that cannot be reversed. The public key is then hashed and encoded into the address that other people send funds to. When you want to spend funds, your wallet software builds a transaction message, stating who is paying whom and how much, and signs it with your private key. Anyone on the network can then use your public key to verify that the signature is valid, without ever seeing the private key itself. The wallet's real job is managing this signing process correctly and keeping the private key away from anyone who should not have it.

Most modern wallets are hierarchical deterministic, or HD, wallets. Rather than generating and separately backing up one key pair at a time, an HD wallet starts from a single random seed, typically shown to the user as a twelve or twenty four word mnemonic phrase, and deterministically derives an entire tree of key pairs from it using a standardized algorithm. This is why writing down twelve words on paper is enough to recover every address a wallet has ever generated, on any compatible wallet software, even years later. It also means that phrase is a single point of failure: anyone who obtains it can derive the same keys and spend the same funds.

A separate and important distinction is custodial versus non-custodial. In a custodial wallet, such as the wallet built into a typical exchange account, the exchange holds the private keys on your behalf and you access your balance through a username and password, much like online banking. In a non-custodial wallet, such as a browser extension wallet, you hold the private key yourself, and no company can freeze or recover it for you. This is the origin of a phrase common in crypto communities: not your keys, not your coins. Custodial wallets trade self custody for convenience and recoverability; non-custodial wallets trade convenience for direct control.

Wallets also differ in how connected they stay to the internet, which the next two chapters take up directly: hot wallets that stay online for convenience, and cold storage that keeps keys offline for security. Every one of these variations is answering a question the blockchain itself cannot answer on its own: who is allowed to move which funds. The wallet, not the blockchain, is where that access control actually lives.
